title: Accessibility Testing
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of accessibility testing in a browser document.
Apply at least one relevant rule from this lesson to a small HTML example.
Check the result using browser inspection, a validator, or an accessibility checklist.

content.intro: This lesson turns “Accessibility Testing” into a practical authoring skill. You will work with keyboard-only testing, understand the choices that matter, and check the result instead of relying on guesswork.
content.why_it_matters: Professional pages need to load efficiently, validate cleanly, adapt to different contexts, and remain understandable to other developers.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Use native HTML semantics first, then test keyboard interaction, visible focus, names, roles, states, headings, and error feedback. Automated checks help but cannot replace manual testing.

items.title: Keyboard-only testing
items.text: Use native HTML semantics first, then test keyboard interaction, visible focus, names, roles, states, headings, and error feedback. Automated checks help but cannot replace manual testing.

items.title: Checking heading hierarchy
items.text: Use heading levels to express document hierarchy rather than to obtain a font size. A logical outline helps people skim and navigate sections.

items.title: Testing form labels
items.text: Associate each control with a persistent label. With an explicit label, the label’s for value must exactly match the control’s id.

items.title: Inspecting accessible names
items.text: Inspecting accessible names is one of the decisions covered by Accessibility Testing. Decide what the markup is meant to communicate, choose the native HTML structure that expresses that meaning, and verify the result in a browser or a relevant validation checklist. Avoid using an element or attribute just because its default appearance seems convenient.

items.title: Using accessibility inspection tools
items.text: Use native HTML semantics first, then test keyboard interaction, visible focus, names, roles, states, headings, and error feedback. Automated checks help but cannot replace manual testing.

items.title: Testing contrast in coordination with CSS
items.text: Use a repeatable loop: reproduce the issue, inspect the source and rendered DOM, read validator or console output, fix one cause, then retest the expected behavior.

items.title: Recognizing the limitations of automated audits
items.text: Recognizing the limitations of automated audits is one of the decisions covered by Accessibility Testing. content_blocks.title: Keep in mind
content_blocks.text: Prefer the native semantic element that communicates intent. Do not choose markup solely for its default visual style.

content.task: Test a short page without relying on color alone: navigate with the keyboard, inspect headings/labels, and write down one improvement.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use the relevant concept from Accessibility Testing.
Keep IDs unique and use valid nesting.
Check the result in a browser and record one finding.
hints: Start with the smallest valid example for accessibility testing.
Add one element or attribute at a time, then check the result.
Compare the source and rendered DOM if the behavior surprises you.
content.expected_output: The page has meaningful header, navigation, main, article, and footer regions.

troubleshooting.symptom: The expected content does not appear.
troubleshooting.check: Confirm the file was saved with an .html extension and inspect its path and nesting.
Check the resolved URL and confirm the referenced file or external resource exists and allows the request.

troubleshooting.symptom: The page looks correct but the markup may be invalid.
troubleshooting.check: Run the Nu Html Checker and follow its first relevant diagnostic, then validate again.

common_mistakes.why: The default appearance is not the element’s main meaning and can make navigation or maintenance harder.
common_mistakes.fix: Choose the element that matches the content purpose, then use CSS for presentation.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a browser’s recovery means the source is valid
common_mistakes.why: Browsers often recover from malformed markup, which can hide defects and produce unexpected document structure.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the rendered DOM and run a validator against the original source.

common_mistakes.why: Missing files, narrow viewports, keyboard access, invalid input, or other states can expose defects.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected state plus one realistic edge case and an accessibility path.

summary: Accessibility Testing is about expressing document structure or behavior intentionally.
Use a repeatable loop: reproduce the issue, inspect the source and rendered DOM, read validator or console output, fix one cause, then retest the expected behavior.
Verify both markup and behavior; do not infer correctness from appearance alone.
